Glenharvie Down

By: Graham Coetzer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As the gold mines closed, and the zama zamas moved in, the picturesque West Rand town of Glenharvie sank into chaos. But one paramedic refuses to give up.

Unique Selling Point:
The picturesque mining town Glenharvie, situated on the West Rand, was once a thriving community. But as many of Sibanye Stillwater's shafts in the area shut down, crime took hold. Residents blame much of it on large groups of zamas waging a turf war for control of the unprotected assets. We have exclusive cctv and cellphone footage showing large groups of armed men running the streets of the town, videos showing shooting incidents where hundreds of rounds are fired, and residents who are at their wits end.

Summary:
Glenharvie is a forgotten West Rand town with a population of just over a few thousand people. Much of the town’s current problems are blamed on two rival gangs of zama zamas operating in the area one from the Welkom area and one group from Stilfontein.

Those problems started when two events coincided. One was the police crackdown in Stilfontein in late 2024 and early 2025, which forced many zamas operating in the area to seek greener pastures. The other was the closure of several gold shafts operated by Sibanye-Stillwater, all within a ten-minute drive of the town. Locals say the place is now run by the zamas, and with a police station manned by only two officials which closes at 4pm everyday, they’ve been left defenceless.

Signs of vandalism and theft can be seen everywhere – hundreds of meters of copper cable dug up and stolen next to busy streets in the centre of town, the local rugby stadium’s pavilion roof is missing all of its corrugated iron roof, and even the police station’s security fence has been stolen.

But dig deeper and the problems are much darker and much more violent. A local paramedic, André Boshoff has seen the violence first hand. His first encounter with zamas was the day they arrived at his neighbour’s home, a local security guard who’d been giving information on the zama zamas to the police and mines. Armed zamas ambushed the guard in his driveway, and opened fire. He was shot and injured. When his wife and daughter came running out of the house, they were both shot and died. Then the zamas walked over to the still living security guard and executed him.

André has decided to fight back. He’s mobilised community patrols and is actively engaging with the mines, municipality and police. But he says the community are fighting a losing battle.

On the 18th of December last year, the war between the two opposing zama factions reached critical mass. They had a massive shootout on the streets of Glenharvie. At least a 100 zamas were involved, some of the shooting was captured on CCTV cameras from local shops. They show armed zamas carrying an assortment of machine guns like AK 47’s. One zama was executed within a few meters of a nursery school.

Adriaan Vos, a local farmer, whose house sits right in the middle of land the zamas use to cross between shafts, was ambushed in the early hours of the morning. When he heard his dogs barking, he went to investigate. A group of men, dressed in the balaclavas and traditional blankets of Basotho zamas, opened fire. André was hit in the knee and the lung. While he lay bleeding, some of the men entered his house and det it on fire. André, the paramedic, responded to the scene. When he got their Adriaan’s whole house was engulfed in flames. André tried to save Adriaan’s beloved dog, who was trapped on the second-floor balcony. He also had several prized parrots in the house. But a gas bottle exploded, and all the animals were engulfed in the flames. Adriaan survived the shooting. He was in hospital for more than a week. Not a single police officer arrived to take a statement. The motif for the attack is unclear. The zamas didn’t steal several vehicles on site. But the night after the fire, they returned and started stripping the farmhouse of copper and steel.

Another farmer was murdered in his farmhouse. This house has since become the base of operations for one of the two groups of zamas. The second group operate from a bush camp behind a hill just outside of town.

We won’t be able to approach them without serious risk, but we can fly a drone over the areas. We do have some footage of the shootings etc. We can accompany André and the other volunteers on a patrol.

We can use André and his attempt at reclaiming the town as the central narrative of a story about a once thriving community being devastated by violent gangs and turf wars. All this after earlier this year, just a few kilometers away in the town of Randfontein, at least 300 people said they were forced out of their homes by zama zamas and took refuge in a local town hall. Meanwhile, in his SONA last month, Pres Cyril Ramaphosa announced deploying the SANDF to Gauteng to combat illegal mining. If they do plan to help out in Glenharvie, they haven’t shown up yet.


Further information:
We have CCTV and Cellphone footage showing shootings, a zama body on the streets of the town etc
We have locations for the two factions of zamas and can fly a drone over the sites

Script:


(Lourensa Eckard) This is a gold mine on the western edge of Gauteng. A large group of men collects gold-bearing rock that has spilled from the conveyor.

(James Wellsted) Since 2013, we’ve been highlighting this as a major issue. We were confronting illegal miners underground. And then also, we’ve had incursions or attempted incursions, into our processing facilities and to our operations.

(Lourensa Eckard) The men appear to retreat – but they’re loading a waiting vehicle. As it drives off, they return and repeat the process. Apparently, with no fear of interruption.

(James Wellsted) It’s the tier one, effectively foot soldiers, in an organised crime cartel. Often when they go to court, they get charged with trespassing. And obviously, with the amount of money that they’re making through illegal mining, they can pay bail very easily. And then they’re back underground within a few hours.

(Lourensa Eckard) Illegal mining: it’s just one of the ills plaguing a once-flourishing mining hub, just an hour’s drive from Johannesburg. This is Glenharvie, a town built on gold – now, forgotten.

(James Wellsted) We’re not going to go back to those heydays unfortunately, because these mines are old; the gold industry is in decline.

(Lourensa Eckard) James Wellsted speaks for Sibanye-Stillwater; the multinational company that’s dominated mining in the area for the last decade. It’s a decade that has brought rapid change: waning gold reserves, vanishing jobs – and an explosion in crime.

(André Boshoff) So, the hijackings picked up.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And as I went through the gate, the gunshots rang out.

(André Boshoff) When you hear the shooting, it’s becoming normal for us.

(Lourensa Eckard) Now, a community under siege ask: are they fighting a losing battle?

(Lourensa Eckard) Bossie, so you are going to take us on a tour of the town?

(André Boshoff) On a little tour of our town – or what’s left of the town.

(Lourensa Eckard) What’s left.

(André Boshoff) Yes.

(Lourensa Eckard) Paramedic André Boshoff, or Bossie, moved to Glenharvie over a decade ago, attracted by its peaceful streets and slow pace. But in his time here, he’s seen it transformed by vandalism and crime.

(Lourensa Eckard) So, it’s this whole trench here? It goes all the way around…

(André Boshoff) The whole trench up until the mine site, they took the cable.

(Lourensa Eckard) And this was the cable that was providing electricity to the town?

(André Boshoff) Yes.

(Lourensa Eckard) Fences stolen, stadium roofs stripped, and copper cable theft on an industrial scale. Not even the police station has been spared.

(André Boshoff) They stole the fence off. When they came back the next morning, half of the fence was gone.

(Lourensa Eckard) Where are the police vehicles? Are they out?

(André Boshoff) No, there’s no vehicle; it’s only those two private vehicles.

(Lourensa Eckard) There’s no permanent police force. Just a part-time satellite station, manned by two officers, that closes in the afternoon. The mining money is dwindling, service delivery is almost non-existent, and residents’ hands are tied. And beneath it all – a more sinister force.

(André Boshoff) It used to be a town full of life, full of children playing in a park. Now, to sit outside with your children, and when you hear the shooting, it’s becoming normal for us.

(Lourensa Eckard) The battle for control raging between two rival groups of zama zamas.

(Lourensa Eckard) A kilogram of zama gold isn’t much bigger than a bar of soap; small enough to slip into your pocket. But given today’s near-record gold prices, it can fetch up to R1.8 million on the black market. And that kind of money is fuelling a violent war that’s no longer underground. It’s spilling onto the streets of local mining communities.

(Lourensa Eckard) The turf war has taken over Glenharvie. Members of the rival gangs walk these streets in broad daylight, brandishing assault rifles. And apparently, unafraid of the authorities.

(André Boshoff) So, I call them Group A and Group B. So, Group B will be on the bottom of the town. The second group is behind where the old mine of Sibanye was.

(Lourensa Eckard) A few months ago, the centre of town erupted in gunfire.

(André Boshoff) Group A invaded Group B’s area. And there was a confrontation and there was a shooting.

(Lourensa Eckard) The two groups entered the town over this hillside, one group chasing another. During the shootout, a fleeing zama was injured.

(André Boshoff) And he took shelter here, because he got shot in his leg. So, they beat him up and they took him down to the road and he got executed here, in the road.

(Lourensa Eckard) They executed him on the side of the road?

(André Boshoff) Executed here in the road. Yes.

(Lourensa Eckard) In broad daylight?

(André Boshoff) In broad daylight.

(Lourensa Eckard) And there’s a crèche just around the corner.

(André Boshoff) The crèche is just down… It’s four houses from here, is the crèche.

(Lourensa Eckard) For the residents of Glenharvie, things like organised crime, syndicates and illegal mining are not theoretical concepts. It means running gun battles through otherwise peaceful roads. It means seeing a dead body on the side of the street. It means living in constant fear over what might happen next.

(Lourensa Eckard) Adriaan Vos, a local farmer, came dangerously close to losing his life.

(Lourensa Subtitles) Tell us what happened the night you were shot at, Vossie?

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) My dogs were barking at the gate. I stood up and went to investigate.

(Lourensa Eckard) He drove around his farm, checking on his animals.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And as I went through the gate, the gunshots rang out. They shot me in my knee and then my bakkie stalled. I bent forward to restart my bakkie, and the shots just kept coming. In the process, I got shot in my back.

(Lourensa Subtitles) [Lourensa] Look at all these holes…

(Lourensa Eckard) Two men fired 17 rounds at Adriaan’s bakkie.

(Lourensa Subtitles) Vossie, so all the shots came from this side?

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, they stood three metres from the bakkie and fired from this side.

(Lourensa Eckard) Miraculously, he managed to get the bakkie started and sped off to a neighbour’s farm. André, who is a member of the community watch, wasn’t on duty that night, – but responded to the incident anyway.

(André Boshoff) We got him there, he was shot. We started stabilising on scene.

(Lourensa Eckard) This footage was filmed the following morning. But this was no ordinary farm attack. On the way to the hospital, the ambulance driver pulled over as he passed Adriaan’s farmhouse.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) They stopped up there by the tar road, opened the door, and I could see my house was on fire.

(Lorensa) Nothing was stolen that night, but Adriaan lost everything. Some of his pets were trapped in the burning building.

(André Boshoff) His animals were crying. I will never forget that the one dog was barking on the second storey. And we couldn’t get close to get the dog out because the fire was too intense. And he collapsed when the floor collapsed of the house.

(André Boshoff) As a medic, that’s something horrific.

(Lourensa Eckard) Adriaan doesn’t know who came for him that night, or why.

(Lourensa Subtitles) Is it sad to see what’s left of your home today?

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, really. I put everything I had into this house. And within hours it was all destroyed.

(Lourensa Eckard) To date, no one has been arrested for the violent attack. But days after leaving hospital, Adriaan found zama zamas looting what was left of his home.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And then there were two shots fired at me again.

(Lourensa Subtitles) They shot at you?

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, then I jumped into my bakkie and left.

(Lourensa Subtitles) How did you know they were zama zamas?

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) I worked on the open-cast mines at Mintails, I know zamas.

(Lourensa Eckard) Even for those who haven’t encountered violence firsthand, it’s a constant, sometimes invisible presence.

(André Boshoff) This road is the old mine road; it connects all the shafts.

(Lourensa Eckard) André pulls over at a so called zama hot zone: this intersection just outside of town, and a road residents no longer dare to drive.

(André Boshoff) There’s informants everywhere, sitting with phones – checking.

(Lourensa Eckard) If we were to drive down this road, do you think we’d survive it?

(André Boshoff) Most probably, not. Let’s go.

(Lourensa Eckard) Helpless and frustrated, some residents blame the mines for not doing more to protect them.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) We told them where they are, what time they arrive, what they do. And it just escalated.

(Lourensa Eckard) But Sibanye say unless they’re called on by police for assistance, their hands are tied.

(James Wellsted) In the townships like Glenharvie – which are actually on proclaimed land which is owned by the municipality effectively – we don’t have any authority. You know, that is actually… It falls under the South African Police Service.

(Lourensa Eckard) If there is a situation at one of your mines near Glenharvie, the closest police station would be the Glenharvie Police Station…

(James Wellsted) Ja.

(Lourensa Eckard) Which is essentially a satellite station.

(James Wellsted) That’s right.

(Lourensa Eckard) I mean, that’s not going to do anything.

(James Wellsted) Well, this is the issue right. So, if we get called in, and we will try and obviously help where we can. But these are very heavily armed gangs; they’re very organised, and they’re getting bigger and bigger and more brazen as time goes on.

(Cell phone video shooting sounds)

(Lourensa Eckard) Just a week before our arrival, this terrified family cowered in their home as a gunbattle between the rival zama factions raged – metres away.

(Cell phone video shooting sounds)

(Lourensa Eckard) Like others in the community, the family stayed off camera, caught in the middle of a deadly war for control of the town’s remaining gold reserves.

(Lourensa Eckard) So, how could anyone realistically fight back?

(André Boshoff) It is a challenge, it’s a big challenge. For us as a community, we did our utmost best here, with the community watch, to make it safe for us, or to try to make it liveable for us.

(Lourensa Eckard) So, why do you do it?

(André Boshoff) I took an oath, as a medic, to protect and to help others that’s in need. And I will do it until I have my last breath.

(Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And as I went through the gate, the gunshots rang out. (André Boshoff) When you hear the shooting, it’s becoming normal for us. (Lourensa Eckard) Now, a community under siege ask: are they fighting a losing battle? (Lourensa Eckard) Bossie, so you are going to take us on a tour of the town? (André Boshoff) On a little tour of our town – or what’s left of the town. (Lourensa Eckard) What’s left. (André Boshoff) Yes. (Lourensa Eckard) Paramedic André Boshoff, or Bossie, moved to Glenharvie over a decade ago, attracted by its peaceful streets and slow pace. But in his time here, he’s seen it transformed by vandalism and crime. (Lourensa Eckard) So, it’s this whole trench here? It goes all the way around… (André Boshoff) The whole trench up until the mine site, they took the cable. (Lourensa Eckard) And this was the cable that was providing electricity to the town? (André Boshoff) Yes. (Lourensa Eckard) Fences stolen, stadium roofs stripped, and copper cable theft on an industrial scale. Not even the police station has been spared. (André Boshoff) They stole the fence off. When they came back the next morning, half of the fence was gone. (Lourensa Eckard) Where are the police vehicles? Are they out? (André Boshoff) No, there’s no vehicle; it’s only those two private vehicles. (Lourensa Eckard) There’s no permanent police force. Just a part-time satellite station, manned by two officers, that closes in the afternoon. The mining money is dwindling, service delivery is almost non-existent, and residents’ hands are tied. And beneath it all – a more sinister force. (André Boshoff) It used to be a town full of life, full of children playing in a park. Now, to sit outside with your children, and when you hear the shooting, it’s becoming normal for us. (Lourensa Eckard) The battle for control raging between two rival groups of zama zamas. (Lourensa Eckard) A kilogram of zama gold isn’t much bigger than a bar of soap; small enough to slip into your pocket. But given today’s near-record gold prices, it can fetch up to R1.8 million on the black market. And that kind of money is fuelling a violent war that’s no longer underground. It’s spilling onto the streets of local mining communities. (Lourensa Eckard) The turf war has taken over Glenharvie. Members of the rival gangs walk these streets in broad daylight, brandishing assault rifles. And apparently, unafraid of the authorities. (André Boshoff) So, I call them Group A and Group B. So, Group B will be on the bottom of the town. The second group is behind where the old mine of Sibanye was. (Lourensa Eckard) A few months ago, the centre of town erupted in gunfire. (André Boshoff) Group A invaded Group B’s area. And there was a confrontation and there was a shooting. (Lourensa Eckard) The two groups entered the town over this hillside, one group chasing another. During the shootout, a fleeing zama was injured. (André Boshoff) And he took shelter here, because he got shot in his leg. So, they beat him up and they took him down to the road and he got executed here, in the road. (Lourensa Eckard) They executed him on the side of the road? (André Boshoff) Executed here in the road. Yes. (Lourensa Eckard) In broad daylight? (André Boshoff) In broad daylight. (Lourensa Eckard) And there’s a crèche just around the corner. (André Boshoff) The crèche is just down… It’s four houses from here, is the crèche. (Lourensa Eckard) For the residents of Glenharvie, things like organised crime, syndicates and illegal mining are not theoretical concepts. It means running gun battles through otherwise peaceful roads. It means seeing a dead body on the side of the street. It means living in constant fear over what might happen next. (Lourensa Eckard) Adriaan Vos, a local farmer, came dangerously close to losing his life. (Lourensa Subtitles) Tell us what happened the night you were shot at, Vossie? (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) My dogs were barking at the gate. I stood up and went to investigate. (Lourensa Eckard) He drove around his farm, checking on his animals. (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And as I went through the gate, the gunshots rang out. They shot me in my knee and then my bakkie stalled. I bent forward to restart my bakkie, and the shots just kept coming. In the process, I got shot in my back. (Lourensa Subtitles) [Lourensa] Look at all these holes… (Lourensa Eckard) Two men fired 17 rounds at Adriaan’s bakkie. (Lourensa Subtitles) Vossie, so all the shots came from this side? (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, they stood three metres from the bakkie and fired from this side. (Lourensa Eckard) Miraculously, he managed to get the bakkie started and sped off to a neighbour’s farm. André, who is a member of the community watch, wasn’t on duty that night, – but responded to the incident anyway. (André Boshoff) We got him there, he was shot. We started stabilising on scene. (Lourensa Eckard) This footage was filmed the following morning. But this was no ordinary farm attack. On the way to the hospital, the ambulance driver pulled over as he passed Adriaan’s farmhouse. (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) They stopped up there by the tar road, opened the door, and I could see my house was on fire. (Lorensa) Nothing was stolen that night, but Adriaan lost everything. Some of his pets were trapped in the burning building. (André Boshoff) His animals were crying. I will never forget that the one dog was barking on the second storey. And we couldn’t get close to get the dog out because the fire was too intense. And he collapsed when the floor collapsed of the house. (André Boshoff) As a medic, that’s something horrific. (Lourensa Eckard) Adriaan doesn’t know who came for him that night, or why. (Lourensa Subtitles) Is it sad to see what’s left of your home today? (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, really. I put everything I had into this house. And within hours it was all destroyed. (Lourensa Eckard) To date, no one has been arrested for the violent attack. But days after leaving hospital, Adriaan found zama zamas looting what was left of his home. (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) And then there were two shots fired at me again. (Lourensa Subtitles) They shot at you? (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) Yes, then I jumped into my bakkie and left. (Lourensa Subtitles) How did you know they were zama zamas? (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) I worked on the open-cast mines at Mintails, I know zamas. (Lourensa Eckard) Even for those who haven’t encountered violence firsthand, it’s a constant, sometimes invisible presence. (André Boshoff) This road is the old mine road; it connects all the shafts. (Lourensa Eckard) André pulls over at a so called zama hot zone: this intersection just outside of town, and a road residents no longer dare to drive. (André Boshoff) There’s informants everywhere, sitting with phones – checking. (Lourensa Eckard) If we were to drive down this road, do you think we’d survive it? (André Boshoff) Most probably, not. Let’s go. (Lourensa Eckard) Helpless and frustrated, some residents blame the mines for not doing more to protect them. (Adriaan Vos Subtitles) We told them where they are, what time they arrive, what they do. And it just escalated. (Lourensa Eckard) But Sibanye say unless they’re called on by police for assistance, their hands are tied. (James Wellsted) In the townships like Glenharvie – which are actually on proclaimed land which is owned by the municipality effectively – we don’t have any authority. You know, that is actually… It falls under the South African Police Service. (Lourensa Eckard) If there is a situation at one of your mines near Glenharvie, the closest police station would be the Glenharvie Police Station… (James Wellsted) Ja. (Lourensa Eckard) Which is essentially a satellite station. (James Wellsted) That’s right. (Lourensa Eckard) I mean, that’s not going to do anything. (James Wellsted) Well, this is the issue right. So, if we get called in, and we will try and obviously help where we can. But these are very heavily armed gangs; they’re very organised, and they’re getting bigger and bigger and more brazen as time goes on. (Cell phone video shooting sounds) (Lourensa Eckard) Just a week before our arrival, this terrified family cowered in their home as a gunbattle between the rival zama factions raged – metres away. (Cell phone video shooting sounds) (Lourensa Eckard) Like others in the community, the family stayed off camera, caught in the middle of a deadly war for control of the town’s remaining gold reserves. (Lourensa Eckard) So, how could anyone realistically fight back? (André Boshoff) It is a challenge, it’s a big challenge. For us as a community, we did our utmost best here, with the community watch, to make it safe for us, or to try to make it liveable for us. (Lourensa Eckard) So, why do you do it? (André Boshoff) I took an oath, as a medic, to protect and to help others that’s in need. And I will do it until I have my last breath.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As the gold mines closed, and the zama zamas moved in, the picturesque West Rand town of Glenharvie sank into chaos. But one paramedic refuses to give up.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The picturesque mining town Glenharvie, situated on the West Rand, was once a thriving community. But as many of Sibanye Stillwater's shafts in the area shut down, crime took hold. Residents blame much of it on large groups of zamas waging a turf war for control of the unprotected assets. We have exclusive cctv and cellphone footage showing large groups of armed men running the streets of the town, videos showing shooting incidents where hundreds of rounds are fired, and residents who are at their wits end.
metadata.Summary: Glenharvie is a forgotten West Rand town with a population of just over a few thousand people. Much of the town’s current problems are blamed on two rival gangs of zama zamas operating in the area one from the Welkom area and one group from Stilfontein. Those problems started when two events coincided. One was the police crackdown in Stilfontein in late 2024 and early 2025, which forced many zamas operating in the area to seek greener pastures. The other was the closure of several gold shafts operated by Sibanye-Stillwater, all within a ten-minute drive of the town. Locals say the place is now run by the zamas, and with a police station manned by only two officials which closes at 4pm everyday, they’ve been left defenceless. Signs of vandalism and theft can be seen everywhere – hundreds of meters of copper cable dug up and stolen next to busy streets in the centre of town, the local rugby stadium’s pavilion roof is missing all of its corrugated iron roof, and even the police station’s security fence has been stolen. But dig deeper and the problems are much darker and much more violent. A local paramedic, André Boshoff has seen the violence first hand. His first encounter with zamas was the day they arrived at his neighbour’s home, a local security guard who’d been giving information on the zama zamas to the police and mines. Armed zamas ambushed the guard in his driveway, and opened fire. He was shot and injured. When his wife and daughter came running out of the house, they were both shot and died. Then the zamas walked over to the still living security guard and executed him. André has decided to fight back. He’s mobilised community patrols and is actively engaging with the mines, municipality and police. But he says the community are fighting a losing battle. On the 18th of December last year, the war between the two opposing zama factions reached critical mass. They had a massive shootout on the streets of Glenharvie. At least a 100 zamas were involved, some of the shooting was captured on CCTV cameras from local shops. They show armed zamas carrying an assortment of machine guns like AK 47’s. One zama was executed within a few meters of a nursery school. Adriaan Vos, a local farmer, whose house sits right in the middle of land the zamas use to cross between shafts, was ambushed in the early hours of the morning. When he heard his dogs barking, he went to investigate. A group of men, dressed in the balaclavas and traditional blankets of Basotho zamas, opened fire. André was hit in the knee and the lung. While he lay bleeding, some of the men entered his house and det it on fire. André, the paramedic, responded to the scene. When he got their Adriaan’s whole house was engulfed in flames. André tried to save Adriaan’s beloved dog, who was trapped on the second-floor balcony. He also had several prized parrots in the house. But a gas bottle exploded, and all the animals were engulfed in the flames. Adriaan survived the shooting. He was in hospital for more than a week. Not a single police officer arrived to take a statement. The motif for the attack is unclear. The zamas didn’t steal several vehicles on site. But the night after the fire, they returned and started stripping the farmhouse of copper and steel. Another farmer was murdered in his farmhouse. This house has since become the base of operations for one of the two groups of zamas. The second group operate from a bush camp behind a hill just outside of town. We won’t be able to approach them without serious risk, but we can fly a drone over the areas. We do have some footage of the shootings etc. We can accompany André and the other volunteers on a patrol. We can use André and his attempt at reclaiming the town as the central narrative of a story about a once thriving community being devastated by violent gangs and turf wars. All this after earlier this year, just a few kilometers away in the town of Randfontein, at least 300 people said they were forced out of their homes by zama zamas and took refuge in a local town hall. Meanwhile, in his SONA last month, Pres Cyril Ramaphosa announced deploying the SANDF to Gauteng to combat illegal mining. If they do plan to help out in Glenharvie, they haven’t shown up yet.
metadata.Further information: We have CCTV and Cellphone footage showing shootings, a zama body on the streets of the town etc We have locations for the two factions of zamas and can fly a drone over the sites
